The same tablet. A court said that was misleading, and the company paid $6 million. Every word and picture in an ad has a job. Can you spot what it's doing?

why.support: You see hundreds of ads a day. Each one wants you to buy something. Learn the tricks, and you decide.
why.core: You see hundreds of ads a day: on your phone, on buses, on packaging, in shops. Each one is designed to make you feel something, want something, and buy it. When you can see the tricks, you can decide for yourself whether it's worth it.
why.extend: Advertising is carefully engineered persuasion. Word choice, tone, images, colour, numbers and design all work to influence an audience. Explaining how these choices work, and what they leave out, lets you judge an ad's claims for yourself.

articles.title: Every word and picture has a job

body.support:
Ads are made by teams whose job is to make you want things. Nothing is there by accident.

**Words**

- **Slogans:** short and catchy.
- **Emotive words:** *delicious, epic, life-changing.*
- **Commands:** *Buy now! Don't miss out!*
- **Science words:** *clinically proven.* Check what they mean.

**Pictures and colours**

- **Happy, cool people.** You link the product with that feeling.
- **Colours:** red means sale. Green means natural.
- **Packaging:** different boxes can make the same thing look different.

**Numbers**

*9 out of 10 people love it!* Nine out of ten of who?

**Tone.** The **tone** is the feeling: fun, calm or urgent. It matches the **audience**.

**Fine print.** The small writing. The catch is often there.

**What's missing?** Ads only show the good side.
body.core:
Ads are made by teams of people whose job is to make you want things. Nothing in an ad is there by accident.

**Words**

- **Slogans:** short, catchy phrases you remember. *“Unleash your legend.”*
- **Emotive words:** words that make you feel something. *Delicious, life-changing, heartbreaking, epic.*
- **Commands:** they tell you what to do. *Buy now. Don't miss out. Try it today.*
- **Questions:** *Tired of being tired?* They make you say yes in your head.
- **Science-y words:** *clinically proven, formula, advanced.* They sound smart, but check what they actually mean.

**Pictures, colours and design**

- **People:** happy, attractive, sporty or cool, so you link the product with feeling that way.
- **Colour:** red and yellow grab attention and say *sale*; green says *natural*; black and gold say *luxury*.
- **Before and after:** shows a change, but was it really the product?
- **Packaging:** different boxes, colours and pictures can make products seem different, even when they're not.

**Numbers**

*9 out of 10 people prefer it!* Nine out of ten of who? How many were asked? *Only $1 a day!* That's $365 a year.

**Tone and audience.** The **tone** of an ad is its feeling: fun, cheeky, calm, serious, urgent or cool. Advertisers choose a tone that suits their **audience**. An energy drink ad for teens is loud and wild. A bank ad for parents is calm and trustworthy.

**Fine print.** The **fine print** is the small writing, often marked with an asterisk (*). It's where the catch usually lives: *conditions apply*, *minimum 24-month contract*, *based on a survey of 20 people*.

**What's missing?** Ads only show the good side. Ask: what aren't they telling me? Price? Side effects? What the cheaper version does?
body.extend:
Advertising is planned persuasion. Teams of specialists choose every element on purpose.

**Language**

- **Slogans:** memorable, repeated phrases.
- **Emotive language:** words chosen to provoke feeling (*indulgent, revolutionary, heartbreaking*).
- **Imperatives:** direct commands (*Buy now. Don't miss out.*).
- **Rhetorical questions:** prompt silent agreement (*Tired of being tired?*).
- **Science-sounding language:** terms like *clinically proven* or *advanced formula*. They sound expert, but may mean very little.

**Visuals and design**

- **People:** attractive, happy or successful people make you link those feelings with the product.
- **Colour:** red and yellow signal urgency or value; green suggests natural; black and gold suggest luxury.
- **Before-and-after images** suggest the product caused the change. That may not be proven.
- **Packaging and branding:** distinct designs can make identical products appear different.

**Numbers.** Statistics persuade, but scrutinise them: *9 out of 10* of how many, chosen how? *Only $1 a day* is $365 a year.

**Tone and audience.** **Tone** (playful, reassuring, urgent, exclusive) is matched to the target **audience**. It's high-energy for young people, and calm and trustworthy for parents or retirees.

**Fine print.** Qualifications often sit in small text after an asterisk: *conditions apply*, contract terms, survey sizes.

**What's left out.** Ads show one side. Ask what's missing: the total cost, the risks, other options, and independent evidence.

caseStudies.title: Four boxes, one tablet

body.support:
**Nurofen** is a painkiller brand.

It sold four products:

- Back Pain
- Period Pain
- Migraine Pain
- Tension Headache.

Each had a different box, colour and picture. It looked like each one was for a different pain.

But all four had the **same medicine** inside.

The **ACCC** took the company to court. The court said the boxes were **misleading**. In **2016**, the company was ordered to pay **$6 million**.

The lesson: packaging is an ad too. Read the ingredients, not just the box.
body.core:
**Nurofen** is a well-known painkiller brand, made by a company called **Reckitt Benckiser**.

In Australia, it sold a range called **Nurofen Specific Pain**. There were four products:

- Back Pain
- Period Pain
- Migraine Pain
- Tension Headache.

Each had its own box, its own colour and its own picture. The packaging made it look like each one was made to treat that type of pain.

But the **ACCC** (the government body that protects consumers) found that all four contained the **same active ingredient**: 342 milligrams of ibuprofen lysine. None was any better at treating one kind of pain than the others.

The ACCC took the company to court. The **Federal Court** found the packaging was **misleading**. At first, the court ordered a penalty of $1.7 million. The ACCC appealed, saying that wasn't enough. In **December 2016**, the **Full Federal Court** raised it to **$6 million**. At the time, the ACCC said it was the biggest penalty for misleading conduct under Australian consumer law.

The lesson: packaging is an ad too. Different colours, words and pictures can make the same thing look different. Read the ingredients, not just the box.
body.extend:
**Nurofen**, made by **Reckitt Benckiser**, is one of Australia's best-known analgesic brands.

Its **Nurofen Specific Pain** range comprised four products: Back Pain, Period Pain, Migraine Pain and Tension Headache. Each had distinct packaging, colours and imagery suggesting it was formulated for that specific pain.

The **ACCC** argued that all four had the **same active ingredient**: 342 mg of ibuprofen lysine. None worked better on its labelled pain than the others.

The **Federal Court** found the packaging **misleading**. It first set a $1.7 million penalty. The ACCC appealed, saying that was too low to stop others doing the same. In **December 2016**, the **Full Federal Court** increased the penalty to **$6 million**, which the ACCC described as the largest penalty for misleading conduct under the Australian Consumer Law at that time. The company's bid to appeal to the High Court was refused in 2017.

The case shows that packaging is advertising. Colours, pictures and labels can create differences that aren't real. Read the ingredients, not the branding.

teacher.overview: Students learn how ads use language (slogans, emotive words, commands, questions, science-y terms), visuals (people, colour, before-and-after, packaging), numbers and fine print to influence an audience, and how tone is chosen for the audience. They annotate a made-up energy drink ad, sort tricks, plan the same ad for different audiences, and hunt for tricks in three real ads, remaking one as an honest truth version. The case study is Nurofen Specific Pain: four differently packaged products with the same active ingredient; in December 2016 the Full Federal Court increased the penalty to $6 million.
prep: Collect catalogues, magazines, packaging and screenshots of ads.
Optional: bring two differently branded products with the same ingredients.
Paper and markers for truth versions.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** e.g. slogans, emotive words, commands, questions, science-y words. People link the product with feelings; colours signal sale, natural or luxury; packaging can make things look different. The feeling of the ad; it's chosen to suit who it's for.

**Ad:** 1 slogan; 2 aspirational picture; 3 science-y claim with asterisk; 4 number trick (10 staff); 5 urgency and command; 6 fine print.

**Sort:** epic camera — words; beach photo — pictures; 4 out of 5 dentists — numbers; $1 a day — numbers; SALE banner — pictures; don't miss out — words.

**Audience (examples):** parents — “Keep the family connected”, family on a couch, warm and reassuring; retirees — “Simple, no surprises”, grandparent video-calling, calm and clear; tradies — “Tough coverage, anywhere”, ute on a work site, practical and strong.

**Case study:** different colours, pictures and pain names; to sell more, by making each one seem specially made for a problem; read the active ingredients.

realityCheck: **Students love this.** Let them bring ads from their own feeds.
**Truth versions get funny.** That's fine; humour shows understanding.
**Keep the medicine case factual.** Don't suggest students avoid medicine; the point is reading the label.
**Works in a real class:** yes. Quick, hands-on and relevant.
